problem: Mapless outdoor/campus navigation from sparse language goals often depends on open-set visual cues such as signs, ramps, crosswalks or detours, and whether a cue matters depends on the plan. Prior approaches fall short in three ways. Feedforward LfD policies (LeLaN, OmniVLA) treat novel and familiar cues alike. Pre-emptive CoT methods (Alpamayo, ECoT) reason over predefined factor categories before any plan exists, so they miss plan-dependent cues. Iterative refinement methods (Inner Monologue, InterPreT, PRoC3S) need human or environment feedback or only refine symbolic plans or code.
motivation: Cue relevance is plan-dependent: a detour matters only if the current plan follows a blocked path, and a sign matters only if visually similar alternative routes exist. Pretrained VLMs can already recognize open-world cues, but they need adaptation to (a) focus on the cues that matter for the current plan and (b) turn critiques into concrete continuous motion updates. SFT alone cannot teach which critiques actually help, because the plan/critique/update space branches quickly. Hand-designed RL rewards are also hard to write for open-world navigation, which motivates a learned preference reward.
key_idea: A single small VLM with role prompts alternates between proposing an image-space waypoint plan and critiquing it in free-form text, then refines the plan conditioned on the critique. The loop is trained with SFT on Gemini-generated oracle critiques, followed by GRPO using a human-preference reward model combined with a Hausdorff expert-alignment reward.
insight: Refinement only helps when both roles are adapted. Mixed planner/critic ablations (A/B = planner/critic) show that ZS/SFT (fine-tuned critic, zero-shot planner) does not reduce error with more refinement steps: the planner cannot turn the critique into motion. SFT/SFT beats SFT/ZS from iteration 0 to 1, so critique quality matters. The reward ablation shows the two reward terms are complementary. The geometric R_exp alone lowers error much less than the combination and causes corner-cutting, because it ignores terrain and semantics. The learned R_phi alone is ineffective, because it accepts acceptable modes rather than the task-optimal one. RL post-training cuts offline planning error by 26% vs SFT. In the real world it adds ~20% success and removes 36% of interventions. Jointly training critic and planner lowers the share of critic-caused failures from 81% (Alpamayo) to 58%. One caveat: with longer RL the planner learns to ignore critiques because its initial plans stop needing refinement, so the best checkpoint comes after 2-3 epochs.
method: Iterative plan–critique CoT: p(ζ_0:K, z_0:K-1 | x) = π_plan(ζ_0|x) ∏ π_plan(ζ_k+1|ζ_k, z_k, x) π_critic(z_k|ζ_k, x). A single shared VLM is prompted as planner or critic. The planner outputs 10 normalized image-space waypoints as JSON. The critic outputs a binary verdict plus a free-form '<fix>' critique referencing at most 2 waypoints. The loop stops when the critic accepts or the budget K is reached (K=1 in practice).

SFT warm-start: a base motion planner is trained to imitate expert image-space plans, then used to sample noisy plans. Gemini-3.1-Flash critiques 5 annotated candidate plans against the expert to produce oracle critiques. The loss supervises three things: the plan from context, the critique given a noisy plan, and the expert plan given noisy plan + critique. Setup: 34,164 training examples, LoRA rank 64 on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct.

Preference reward model R_φ: initialized from the SFT VLM with a linear head on the penultimate hidden state. It is trained with a Bradley-Terry loss on human rankings: 1150 samples × 5 candidate plans, single annotator, 1–5 relative ranking, ties discarded. It scores only (context, plan), not the critique history.

Hybrid reward: R = R_φ + λ R_exp, where R_exp = clip(1 − (4/√2)·d_H(ζ, ζ̂), −1, 1) and d_H is the symmetric Hausdorff distance to the expert plan in normalized image space. Weights are 0.8 (R_φ) / 0.2 (R_exp).

GRPO post-training in the loop: sample one shared initial plan ζ_0 per context, then G=8 critique+refinement rollouts. Each rollout is scored by the reward of its final plan, advantages are group-normalized, and the KL penalty (β=0.01) is taken to the frozen SFT policy. This co-trains critic and planner. It is justified by a Donsker–Varadhan argument: raising expected reward improvement raises a lower bound on the information gain a critique induces.

Grounding policy π_gnd (following VENTURA): a frozen DepthAnythingV2 encoder of the current RGB and a finetuned EfficientNet-B0 encoder of the boolean plan-overlay image are concatenated channel-wise. A spatial softmax (384 keypoints × 384 features) feeds an 8-layer/8-head transformer that outputs 10 Cartesian xyz waypoints (test MSE 0.018 m). The waypoints are tracked by a pure-pursuit controller on Boston Dynamics Spot, and the model is re-queried after each plan.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (LoRA fine-tuned with SFT + GRPO; shared planner/critic), plus a trained grounding policy (frozen DepthAnythingV2 encoder + EfficientNet-B0 + transformer)
setting.training_data: SCAND plus 1.5 h of teleoperated instruction-following demos (Foresight dataset: 88 missions, 25 urban/campus environments). SFT set: 34,164 train / 6,009 val examples. Language instructions and oracle critiques were generated by Gemini-3.1-Flash. Preference data: 1 h of demos, 1150 samples × 5 ranked trajectories. RL uses only the Foresight dataset.
setting.observation: monocular RGB history (4 frames at 224×392) from an Azure Kinect, plus a natural-language instruction; robot odometry is used for control
setting.action_space: 10 normalized image-space waypoints, grounded to 10 Cartesian xyz waypoints and tracked by a pure-pursuit controller
setting.simulator: real world only (offline evaluation on held-out real-world dataset + Boston Dynamics Spot deployments)

numbers_note: No standard VLN/ObjectNav benchmark is used. The offline evaluation (Hausdorff distance to the expert in BEV, 984 held-out samples from the Foresight dataset, averaged over 12 rollouts) appears only in figures, including comparisons to Gemini-ER1.6, Alpamayo, zero-shot Qwen3-VL and the reward/recipe ablations. The text gives only relative figures: RL reduces final planning error by 26% vs SFT, and critic-failure share falls from 81% to 58% vs Alpamayo. The headline '37% success improvement / 52% fewer interventions' is an aggregate over the real-world table.
results: Across 6 real-world Spot environments, Foresight succeeds in 7/8 sign-understanding, 7/8 structural-clue and 6/8 detour trials, with 0.71 / 1.14 / 1.00 interventions per mission. The strongest baseline, a reproduced Alpamayo (structured Chain-of-Causation on the same Qwen3-VL-2B), gets 4/8, 3/8 and 4/8 with 2.00 / 1.67 / 2.00 interventions; LeLaN gets 1/8, 2/8 and 2/8. The paper summarizes this as +37% task success and −52% interventions. Offline, even the SFT-only Foresight beats Gemini-ER1.6 and Alpamayo after one refinement. RL post-training lowers planning error by a further 26%, and in the real world adds ~20% success with 36% fewer interventions than SFT-only. The loop runs at ~3.05 s per plan–critique iteration on a Jetson AGX Orin, vs 5.82 s for Alpamayo.
limitations: Outcome-level reward gives weak credit assignment across critique vs. critique-following. Late in RL the planner learns to ignore critiques, so the best checkpoint comes after only 2-3 epochs. The model also tends to over-refine plans that need no change.
No long-horizon memory or multi-view reasoning, so cues seen only briefly can be lost. Evaluation covers only static environments; dynamic scenes and faster inference (~3 s per loop) are left open.
Evaluation is small-scale: 4 trials per environment, 6 environments, a self-collected offline dataset, and preference labels from a single annotator. There are no standard-benchmark numbers.
